title: Loadgen traffic sculpting and repeatability manifest
content:
Purpose:
This doc is a pragmatic, experiment-first manifesto for running throughput benchmarks that are both meaningful and repeatable on the serving runtime. It synthesizes lessons from chaotic runs, production traces, and previous bench playbooks and emphasizes a traffic-sculpting approach: explicitly construct and control input characteristics, noise sources, and priming so runs are diagnosable and comparable across hardware and software changes.

Scope and goals:
- Primary goal: measure sustained token/sec throughput at a target p50/p95 latency SLO with guarded repeatability (>=3 runs within 3% for non-thermal variance).
- Secondary goals: identify dominant bottlenecks (CPU vs GPU vs host memory vs PCIe), expose sensitivity to sequence-length and batch mix, and capture warmup artifacts.
- Not goal: micro-optimizing single-request latency tail outliers; this is throughput-first instrumentation.

Guiding principles (short):
1) Sculpt inputs: generate explicit distributions for sequence length, prompt tokens, and response token budgets. Avoid opaque "prod-like" blobs unless fingerprinted.
2) Enumerate noise: list and, where possible, disable cross-traffic, system cron jobs, telemetry exporters, NTP jitter, and background OS updates.
3) Anchor to deterministic observables: capture GPU utilization, SM clocks, CPU steal, cgroup throttling, NIC interrupts, and kernel scheduling counters.
4) Warmup then measure windows: separate micro-bench warmups, SLO validation, and long steady windows.
5) Version and seed everything that can be seeded. If seeding not possible, call it out and use statistical anchors.

Load generator profiles (recommended canonical set):
- tiny-chat (low tokens/request): seq_in 8–32, max_out 16, concurrency range for steady-state 64–512, target QoS: p50<40ms. Use for high-concurrency path profiling.
- medium-dialog (mixed): seq_in 32–128, max_out 128, concurrency 8–64. Matches interactive assistants.
- long-completion (expensive): seq_in 128–512, max_out 512, concurrency 1–8. Stresses KV cache and attention memory.
- burst-mix (microbursts): Poisson bursts with lambda=0.8, peak multiplier=8, floor=1. Capture queueing and backpressure.

Each profile is defined by an explicit JSON blob in our harness (example):
{
  "profile_name": "medium-dialog",
  "arrival_process": "poisson",
  "seq_in_dist": "zipf:1.2:32:128",
  "max_out": 128,
  "client_concurrency": 32,
  "rng_seed": 43109
}

Repeatability recipe (workflow):
1) Provision identical hosts or isolate single-GPU node. Record kernel, driver, and firmware versions.
2) Bootstrap: disable periodic telemetry exports, pause OS updates, set governor to performance, pin interrupts to dedicated CPU where possible. Log these changes.
3) Thermal baseline: run a short 10m low-load pass (tiny-chat) to record idle temps; if temps > 70C pre-run, schedule cooldown.
4) Seeded warmup: run the profile with the harness RNG seed and deterministic client emulator for N=2k requests or 10 minutes (whichever first). Purpose: populate KV cache and JITs.
5) Controlled cooldown: 2m idle.
6) Measurement windows: run 3x measurement runs of length M (recommended 30m for long-completion, 10–15m for medium/tiny), separated by 5m cooldowns.
7) Validation: runs pass if throughput and p50/p95 fall within experimental tolerances and GPU clocks and temps are stable across the window.

Warmup strategy details (observations + heuristics):
- Seedless warmup is fragile: many microbenchmarks that claimed "seedless warmup" produced 6–9% throughput delta across runs. We recommend always choosing a seed in harness when comparing code changes.
- Priming queries: use a small, well-chosen set of canonical prompts for attention / KV paths to exercise both short and long context. Keep set stable in repo.
- Progressive ramping: prefer ramp-to-target over instantaneous spikes. Ramping schedule example: 0% -> 25% -> 50% -> 75% -> 100% over 5 minutes with hold of 60–120s at 100% before measurement starts. This reduces transient oscillation and evens thermal response.

Noise catalog and mitigation checklist (non exhaustive):
- System noise: NTP drift, automatic log rotate, cron jobs. Mitigate: suspend/coordinate, run in isolated test tenancy.
- Container noise: background daemons in same cgroup. Mitigate: run dedicated container or bare-metal.
- Network noise: ARP/neighbor scans, management plane traffic. Mitigate: isolate NIC, remove nonessential routes.
- Telemetry and observability agents: sampling exporters can create CPU spikes. Mitigate: lower retention/buffer sizes, or disable for bench.
- Power management: DVFS interactions. Mitigate: set CPU and GPU to fixed performance profiles.

Instrumentation: what to capture every run (minimum):
- Loadgen: per-second requests, per-second tokens emitted, client-side latencies (p50/p95/p99), RNG seed, profile name.
- Node: nvidia-smi sampling (1s), GPU temps, power, SM util, memory util.
- Host: top/cpuacct, interrupts, softirq, iowait, IRQ affinity.
- Network: interface drops, tx/rx bytes, tx queue length.
- Runtime specific: KV cache hit rate per-session, per-model mem footprint, offload counts, compilation events.

Analysis heuristics (quick):
- If throughput regresses but GPU util unchanged: look at CPU steal, cgroup preemption, or async copy stalls.
- If p95 spikes while mean throughput stable: suspect head-of-line blocking from large requests — re-run with shard-aware throttling.
- If runs vary >5% across repeats: re-check thermal curve and background interrupts; increase measurement window.

Quick-run commands and knobs (example invocations):
- harness run --profile medium-dialog --seed 43109 --ramp 300 --measure 1200 --cooldown 300 --n-runs 3
- capture: metric-exporter --samples-per-second 1 --gpu --host --outfile run-{{ts}}.tar.gz

Repro checklist (preflight):
- [ ] hardware + driver versions logged
- [ ] governor/perf modes set and documented
- [ ] harness seed present and checked into test vector repo
- [ ] telemetry disabled or throttled for run window
- [ ] baseline idle temps recorded
- [ ] priming queries and prompt set versioned
- [ ] measurement window and cooldown durations agreed

Common pitfalls and practical notes: 
- "Prod-like" traffic is useful for system debugging, but for performance claims you must first map prod fingerprint into small orthogonal axes (seq length, response size, concurrency). Claiming a single prod-like run is representative is a recipe for nondeterminism.
- Avoid heavy use of synthetic random long-tail sequences unless you track their fingerprints; these can introduce variance that masks real fixes.
- Quantization / mixed-precision toggles should be evaluated independently with identical warmup/priming.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Investigate adaptive ramp schedules driven by real-time thermal telemetry to shorten cooldowns without sacrificing repeatability.
- Add hardware-level event sampling (perf/PTA) integration in harness to correlate stalls with host events.

Appendix: immediate to-do for next iteration:
1) Add a canonical priming-set file in the repo and link PR for review (Ethan owning).
2) Implement a small harness feature to assert GPU clocks remain pinned during measurement and fail otherwise.
3) Draft a CI gate that runs a 15m medium-dialog profile on dedicated infra for every release candidate and stores artifacts.

Notes to self: captures from Slack channel #bench-harness. Several runs in Jan had hidden telemetry turned on (observability-agent 2.1) which caused a 7% variation in throughput on A100 nodes; reproduce and file ENG-2314.
